name: Mendoza
description: High-altitude Malbec at the foot of the Andes: violet, black plum and velvet tannin, grown where the vines sit up to a mile above sea level.
funFact: Malbec is originally a Bordeaux grape that nearly disappeared in France after frost in 1956; Argentina had already made it the national grape, and it now grows more Malbec than the rest of the world combined.

serve.how: Serve slightly below room temperature in a large glass. Altitude gives these wines both intense colour and a fine, powdery tannin that shows best with a little air, so decant young bottles for thirty minutes. The floral violet note is the marker of good Mendoza Malbec and fades if the wine is served too warm.

composition.summary: High-altitude Malbec grown on alluvial soils in the Andean rain shadow.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Malbec, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Bonarda alongside.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Mendoza province at 800–1,500 metres in the Andean foothills.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Destemmed and fermented warm, with moderate extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak, often partly new.

composition.process: Intense high-altitude sunlight thickens skins and builds colour and tannin, while cold nights preserve the acidity and floral aromatics.

name: Valle de Uco
description: Mendoza's coldest, highest sub-region, climbing past 1,500 metres. Tighter, more mineral and more structured than the valley floor below.
funFact: Parts of the Uco Valley sit above 1,500 metres, high enough that hail nets are standard equipment and the growing season runs weeks behind vineyards an hour away.

serve.how: Decant for an hour — Uco Malbec is markedly more structured than lower-altitude Mendoza and needs air to unwind. Serve cool in a large glass. The wines reward keeping; a bottle at five to eight years shows the stony, herbal character that altitude gives and that young bottles hide behind fruit.

composition.summary: Very high-altitude Malbec on stony alluvial soils, cooler and firmer than valley-floor Mendoza.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Malbec, with Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay planted alongside.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Uco Valley, at 1,000–1,700 metres in the Mendoza pre-cordillera.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Careful, cooler fermentation with restrained extraction to protect freshness.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak, often with a portion of concrete or amphora.

composition.process: Extreme altitude slows ripening and preserves acidity, producing tighter, stonier wines that need more bottle age than warmer Mendoza sites.

name: Cafayate
description: Torrontés grown at nearly two thousand metres in the Calchaquí valleys — intensely floral on the nose and, unexpectedly, bone dry on the palate.
funFact: Some Cafayate vineyards sit above 2,000 metres, among the highest commercial vineyards on earth, where ultraviolet intensity is strong enough to thicken grape skins measurably.

serve.how: Serve well chilled — the aromatics are so forward that a warm glass tips into perfume. The classic surprise is the gap between nose and palate: it smells sweet and finishes dry, so pair it as a dry white rather than an aromatic off-dry one. Drink young; Torrontés loses its florals within a couple of years.

composition.summary: High-altitude aromatic Torrontés fermented dry in stainless steel.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Torrontés Riojano.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Calchaquí Valleys around Cafayate in Salta, at 1,700–2,000 metres.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless-steel fermentation to preserve the floral aromatics.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: No oak; bottled young for freshness.

composition.process: Extreme altitude and intense ultraviolet light build powerful floral aromatics, which cold stainless fermentation captures before bottling the wine dry and young.

name: Colchagua Valley
description: Chile's warm heartland for Carmenère and Cabernet: ripe, dark and softly herbal, with the green-pepper note that gives the grape away.
funFact: Carmenère was believed extinct after phylloxera until 1994, when a French researcher realised Chile's 'Merlot' had been Carmenère all along — the country had been growing a lost Bordeaux grape for a century without knowing.

serve.how: Serve slightly cool in a large glass, and decant a young bottle for half an hour. The signature green-peppercorn note is a varietal marker rather than a fault, but it becomes vegetal if the wine is served too cold, so avoid over-chilling. It softens considerably with a few years in bottle.

composition.summary: Warm-climate Carmenère and Cabernet Sauvignon on alluvial valley soils.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Carmenère and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Syrah alongside.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Colchagua Valley in Chile's Rapel region, warmed and sheltered from the Pacific.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Warm fermentation with extended maceration for colour and body.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French and American oak.

composition.process: A warm, dry growing season ripens Carmenère fully — essential, since underripe fruit turns aggressively green — and extended maceration builds the dark, soft-tannined style.

name: Maipo Valley
description: Chile's oldest fine-wine valley, on Santiago's doorstep: Cabernet with a distinctive minty, dusty edge that locals attribute to the Andes above it.
funFact: The minty-eucalyptus note in Maipo Cabernet is so consistent that it functions as a regional signature, and it appears in wines from vineyards with no eucalyptus trees anywhere near them.

serve.how: Decant young bottles for an hour. Serve cool in a large glass so the mint and cedar sit alongside the cassis rather than dominating. Alto Maipo wines from higher up the Andean slope are firmer and repay a decade in bottle; valley-floor wines drink well much sooner.

composition.summary: Andean-influenced Cabernet Sauvignon from Chile's most established fine-wine valley.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and Carmenère.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Maipo Valley south of Santiago, rising into the Andean foothills at Alto Maipo.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Destemmed, fermented warm with long maceration.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–24 months in French oak, a portion new.

composition.process: Warm days and cold Andean nights build ripe blackcurrant fruit over firm acidity, with long maceration and oak ageing giving the cedar and structure.

name: Casablanca Valley
description: Chile's cool coastal valley, planted only since the 1980s: crisp Sauvignon Blanc with grapefruit bite and a distinctly saline finish.
funFact: Casablanca was considered too cold to ripen grapes until the 1980s, when growers proved otherwise; it is now the reference point for Chilean white wine and barely thirty years old as a region.

serve.how: Serve well chilled in a standard white glass. The salinity that marks coastal Chilean Sauvignon shows best cold, and the grapefruit sharpens rather than softens as the wine warms. Drink young — these are made for freshness and lose their edge after two or three years.

composition.summary: Cool coastal Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay under strong Pacific influence.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, with some Pinot Noir.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Casablanca Valley between Santiago and the Pacific, cooled by coastal fog.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless-steel fermentation, protecting aromatics from oxygen.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little or no oak; brief lees contact for texture.

composition.process: Morning fog and cold Pacific air slow ripening dramatically, holding acidity while the aromatic compounds develop, and stainless fermentation preserves both.

name: Itata Valley
description: Chile's oldest vineyards and its newest fashion: ungrafted País and Cinsault, dry-farmed on granite by smallholders, made without makeup.
funFact: País arrived with Spanish missionaries in the sixteenth century and was Chile's dominant grape until the 1990s, when it was dismissed as peasant wine — the same old bush vines are now the country's most sought-after fruit.

serve.how: Serve cool, closer to cellar temperature than room temperature — these are light, high-acid reds that turn thin and sour if served warm. Use a wide glass. Many are made with minimal sulphur and little filtration, so expect some sediment and treat an open bottle as a two-day proposition.

composition.summary: Light, dry-farmed reds from old ungrafted País and Cinsault bush vines on granite.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: País and Cinsault, some over a century old and ungrafted.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Itata Valley in southern Chile, on decomposed granite, farmed without irrigation.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Whole-cluster and semi-carbonic fermentation with native yeast.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Old barrels, concrete or tank; little or no new oak.

composition.process: Ancient dry-farmed bush vines on granite give low yields of high-acid fruit, fermented with native yeast and minimal intervention to make deliberately light, fresh reds.

name: Serra Gaúcha
description: Brazil's sparkling heartland, settled by Italian immigrants: traditional-method fizz with tropical fruit brightness and unusually high natural acidity.
funFact: Brazilian sparkling wine has quietly won a string of international blind tastings, helped by a humid climate that keeps acidity high — the same humidity that makes still red wine difficult there.

serve.how: Serve well chilled in a tulip rather than a narrow flute, which traps the brioche aroma. Pour at an angle to preserve the mousse. These are made in the traditional method with real lees ageing, so treat them as you would Cava or Crémant rather than as a simple party fizz.

composition.summary: Traditional-method sparkling wine from a humid subtropical highland region.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling Itálico.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Serra Gaúcha highlands of Rio Grande do Sul, settled by Italian immigrants from the 1870s.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Traditional method — secondary fermentation in bottle.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–24 months on lees before disgorgement.

composition.process: High humidity and cool highland nights keep acidity unusually high, which suits secondary bottle fermentation and gives the wines their tension.
